generatedProse.concept-context: Getting the most out of a psychology placement is a matter of initiative across three phases. Before you start, prepare: set your aims, read up on the setting, and agree with your supervisor how they can help. While you are there, engage: volunteer for data collection or analysis, ask why a measure or protocol was chosen, watch how experienced psychologists work with clients or participants, and seek feedback early. Afterwards, consolidate: record what you did and learned, and connect it to your development and your applications.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students spend a term on the same research project placement.

Tom waits to be given jobs and does them well enough. When a coding scheme is unclear, Tom guesses rather than asks, and never requests feedback for fear of seeming unsure. The work passes, but no one stretches him, and the placement ends much as it began.

Amara asks, on the first day, what would make the term useful to the research team, and volunteers to help design part of the analysis, just beyond her current skill. When a protocol is unclear, she checks early; after each piece of work, she asks what could be stronger. By the end, Amara has done harder work, learned faster, and is remembered when a reference is needed.

Same project, same length. Amara took the initiative that turned time into learning.
generatedProse.summary: You get the most out of a psychology placement by being proactive across three phases: preparing and aiming before, taking initiative and seeking feedback during, and recording and connecting afterwards. You can now apply these strategies, tell a proactive approach from a passive one, and choose an active move when you are in the thick of it. The last lesson is about showing what all this produced: how practice is assessed, and how to evidence your learning.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's term more productive than Tom's?

items.text: She took the initiative: asking, volunteering for stretch, and seeking feedback early.
She was given easier tasks that were simpler to complete.
She avoided asking questions so as not to seem unsure.
She waited to be told exactly what to do at each step.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara took the initiative, asking, volunteering and seeking feedback, which turned the term into learning.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did rather than waited for.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's term was more productive because she took the initiative: asking, volunteering for stretch and seeking feedback early, rather than waiting, playing safe or guessing.
